title: C: Storing a List of Names
description: Holding several names in a 2D char array and filling them with a loop.
congratsText: Well done. You can now store a list of names, tell a row apart from the whole grid, and pass either one where it belongs.
objectives: Declare a 2D char array that holds several names
Fill every row using a loop and a one-name function
Pass a whole grid into a function that prints the list
recap: char names[3][20] is 3 rows of 20 letters; one row holds one name.
names[i] is a single row, so a one-name function fills it unchanged.
One index picks the row; two indexes pick a single letter inside that row.
A grid parameter is written char list[][20] — the row width cannot be left out.

sections.title: A List of Names Is a Grid

chunks.text: char names[3][20]; is 3 rows, each row holding up to 20 letters. One row holds one name.

check.question: How many names can char names[3][20]; hold?

chunks.text: The first number is how many names. The second is how long each one may be — they do very different jobs.

check.question: In char names[3][20], what does the 20 control?
options: How long each name can be
How many names fit in total

chunks.text: Starting every row at "none" is a habit worth keeping — an unfilled row then says so instead of showing leftover memory.

check.question: Why start each row at "none" before filling it?
options: An empty row is then obvious
C refuses to run without it

quiz.question: Nothing else has run yet. What does this print?
options: Nothing at all, the row is empty

chunks.text: names[i] is not a letter — it is a whole row, which means one complete name.
Because a row is just a name, a function written for one name works on it with no edits: getName(names[i]);.

check.question: Does getName need rewriting to work on a list of names?
options: No, it is handed one row
Yes, lists need their own version

chunks.text: Wrap that call in a loop and the whole list fills: three turns of the loop means three different rows handed over, one at a time.

check.question: The loop runs 3 times calling getName(names[i]). How many rows get filled?
options: Three, a different one each turn
One, the same row every turn

quiz.question: Type the exact word this prints.

chunks.text: Read the brackets left to right: the first picks the row, the second picks the letter inside that row.

check.question: In names[2][0], what does the 2 pick?

chunks.text: So names[0] prints with %s as a whole word, while names[0][0] prints with %c as a single letter.

check.question: Row 0 holds Maria. What is in names[0][0]?

chunks.text: Dropping the row index is the classic slip. getName(names) hands over the whole grid, not a row, and every answer lands in row 0.

check.question: getName(names) is called three times. Which rows get filled?
options: All three rows, one per call

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to build a function that prints every name in the list.

chunks.text: A function that prints the whole list needs the whole grid, so its parameter is written char list[][20].

check.question: showNames prints every name. What must it be given?

chunks.text: The [20] cannot be left out. Without the row width, C cannot tell where one name ends and the next begins.

check.question: Why must the 20 stay in char list[][20]?
options: C needs it to find each row
It sets how many rows exist

chunks.text: Nothing is returned, and nothing needs to be. The grid arrives as an address, so the function reads and writes the real list in main().

check.question: Does showNames need a return line to give the list back?
options: No, it used the real grid
Yes, or the list is lost

quiz.question: The [i] was left out of the getName call. What prints?
